subject: Errors in stratified analysis in Distance R package

messages.author: cf57d36d0970fcb6
messages.subject: Errors in stratified analysis in Distance R package
parts:
Hello,

I'm relatively new to both distance sampling and R and am running in to some issues with my analysis of Antarctic Prion burrows on Macquarie Island:
  1. I can't get the code for fitting a ddf in the worked example Multiple covariate detection function (MCDS) analysis of crabeater seals (.Rmd, data) working. It keeps returning the following error: Error in `contrasts<-`(`*tmp*`, value = contr.funs[1 + isOF[nn]]) : contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels. R tells me that the variable I am trying to query is a factor with 2 levels, so I'm not sure what is going on.
  2. When trying to fully stratify my data following the example Stratified study region for minke whales in the Southern Ocean (.Rmd, data) I run into an issue that 2 of 8 strata have too few detections to fit detection functions. This means when I come to add up all the AIC values to compare with AIC values for models using stratum as a covariate and of pooled data I'm effectively missing two values. Basically the results seem incomparable so I for the remainder of the analysis I've gone with the model using stratum as a covariate.
  3. When I come to try to generate density and abundance estimates for each stratum something weird is going on. In the table generated the total Effort comes out as 262 (presumably km) but only 157 km of transect were completed. 
  4. In the abundance estimate generated one stratum was barely sampled because it was essentially unsuitable cliff habitat. But in the short area sampled 3 detections were made. This results in a massively high density estimate for the stratum and a huge and inaccurate overall contribution to the overall population estimate.
  5. It strikes me as odd that nowhere does the analysis appear to require information on transects along which no burrows were detected. This is obviously very important when estimating overall density/abundance within a stratum.
Sorry for such a long list. I've attached my data, R code, and an additional file with all transect info which includes those transects along which no burrows were detected.

If I can figure all of this out I'd like to move on to applying density surface models to my data. Thanks for a great set of R packages.

Jez

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Errors in stratified analysis in Distance R package
parts:
Jez

I have not yet taken a look at the files you sent along, but I'll make comments about your items 1 and 5; returning to the rest at another time.

1) I just ran the crabeater seal analysis using the R markdown file on the distancesampling.org website.  I could not duplicate the error dealing with `contrasts` you describe.  Could it be that you are not using the most current versions of the packages?  I get this result in the R console when running the code:

> library(Distance)
Loading required package: mrds
This is mrds 2.2.0
Built: R 3.5.2; ; 2019-01-21 17:49:30 UTC; windows

5) Your data *should* include information on transects without detections.  The lack of detections is important information for the analysis.  Without properly accounting for survey effort, even when no detections are made, the encounter rate (fundamental to density estimation) is incorrect.  If you examine the minke whale data associated with the second vignette (and your issue 2), you will see several transects in the data file on which no minke whales were detected (South stratum: transects 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12; North stratum: 17 and 23).

2) I'll look through your data, but it is not uncommon for some strata to have too few detections to meaningfully fit a detection function.

3) Wikipedia tells me the island is 35km x 5km.  I'm guessing that getting 262 or 157km of survey effort (which is the correct value?) is because of multiple traverses of transects.  Correct?

4) You may wish to reconsider whether the stratum that received so little sampling effort should be included in your study area.

More later...

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Errors in stratified analysis in Distance R package
parts:
Jez

I've spent a bit of time with your data, and I need your help to understand your survey design and data organisation.

> head(prions)
  Study.area Region.Label     Area Sample.Label     Effort distance size slope veg_height observer
1       2515            5 16.64778            1 0.03361597      0.3    1     D          S       PP
2       2515            5 16.64778            2 0.03361597      0.5    1     D          S       PP

Conventionally, the first field, Study.area, represents the name of the study area, hence there is customarily a single value for all records.  I don't know the rationale for different values for study.area.

For region.label, you have 8 unique values, which makes sense.  Half of the strata have <35 detections (strata 1, 4, 5, and 7)

I presume the units in which region area is specified is km^2 (because the total of the 8 stratum areas is roughly the size of the island).

Sample.Label confuses me, because the

> length(unique(prions$Sample.Label))
[1] 2605

This is two orders of magnitude larger than the number of transects we are accustomed to seeing in a survey.  And the lengths of the transects (units km?) are also surprisingly small 33m?  You noted in your email you were hoping eventually to construct density surface models; have you specified segmented transects as the samples here?

Distance is, hopefully, the perpendicular distance to the burrows.  However, the units of measure for perpendicular distance is not consistent with the units of measure for region area and transect length.  That is why the covered area in the model output vastly exceeds the size of the island.  Best to convert distance units to km as well.  Out of curiosity, how large in diameter are the burrows?  I note your measurements are to the nearest 10cm(?).  Is this the distance to the burrow entrance centre?  That would be best.

I have nothing to say about your item 3) where you suggest total effort in the data does not match your belief that 157km were surveyed.  Nor do I have comments regarding transects without detections.  As I noted earlier, all survey effort needs to be recorded in the data, even effort that did not result in detections.

Think of the data organisation of a line transect survey in a hierarchical fashion:

A single study area divided (perhaps) into strata.  Within each stratum, there are transects.  On (most/some) transects there are detections.  This will permit estimation of density/abundance from a design-based perspective.  If preparing to use density surface models, transects are subdivided into segments; but the hierarchy remains in that under that situation, detections belong to segments.

Once we are on the same page, then we can make progress.

parts:
Dear Eric,

Thanks again for your help last week. I've gone back and reorganised the data and am making progress. The fundamental issue was that I hadn't included all of the transects on which no burrows were detected. I have now done so and have got the analysis working. The overall effort is coming out correct at 157 km of transects. 

In the field 217 transects totaling 157 km were walked. I have indeed segmented these transects, first based upon vegetation height recorded in the field which I would like to use as a covariate in the analysis, and second when overlaying them on a GIS classification layer of 8 strata across the island. This resulted in ~3,500 transect sections to feed into the analysis. Is there any issue with doing it this way? I can't see an alternative if I want to be able to calculate stratum-specific density and abundance estimates.

So I've effectively run my data through the first example from the website (duck nests) and the second (minkes). I'm struggling slightly with introducing covariates into the analysis:
  • For some reason the code: 
    • prions.ddf <- ddf(method="ds", dsmodel=~mcds(key="hr", formula=~observer), data=prions.fixed$data, meta.data=list(width=0.005)) 
    • is still returning an Error in `contrasts<-`(`*tmp*`, value = contr.funs[1 + isOF[nn]]) : contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels
    • I've updated my versions of R and Distance so I'm not sure if there's an issue with how I've set my data up. I can't track down the crabbieMCDS.csv to run in R - could that be an issue with my machine pointing towards a different working directory.
  • I'm not sure how to introduce multiple covariates before model testing. Partly, the worked examples show how to introduce one covariate e.g. side of plane but I'm not sure how to add additional code to include additional covariates in the same model. I'm not sure whether a stepwise approach to model testing is better i.e. adding one covariate at a time, or adding them all in in different combinations and seeing which model comes out the best overall i.e. hazard rate including stratum and observer, hazard rate including stratum, observer and veg height etc. I have few enough covariates that it is probably possible to do all combinations and select the best.
I've attached my revised dataset and code. If you're aware of any worked examples that tackle multiple covariates I'm very happy to do more digging myself. 

Many thanks again,
Jez

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Errors in stratified analysis in Distance R package
parts:
Jez

Happy to read you have found your missing effort.  I worry that effort not accounted for by analysts who ignore transects without detections is more common that acknowledged.  Here are a variety of comments based on your last email.

To your model fitting problem:

You cannot use the function ddf() because ddf() expects fields in your data (object, detected) that you do not have.  The function ds() in the Distance package circumvents this problem. 

Regarding the problems with model fitting: there are still problems with your data file, for many observations, the observer covariate is missing, causing complaints from the ds() function.  Examining your csv file with a text editor reveals

The other thing to know about ds() and ddf() is they were designed with "double observer" surveys in mind.  Hence the field name "observer" carried special meaning for these functions.  Renaming the final field in your data something other than "observer" resolves the error you were having.

names(prions)[10] <- "whom"

prion.observer <- ds(prions, truncation=prion.trunc,
                      key="hn",  formula=~whom)

Use of multiple covariates and modelling philosophy

Distance sampling, unlike mark-recapture, has the property of model robustness, meaning that unbiased estimates are still obtained even if not all sources of variability in detection are incorporated. Hence, it is not common to fit an exhaustive candidate model set to data.  We have lectures and exercises on the use of covariates in detection function modelling found at

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/

There you can find discussion of modelling strategies with covariates and examples of such analyses

Designs for stratum-specific abundance estimates

The approach you have taken with your design, to cut across habitat types with continuous transects, and essentially post-stratify after data collection is a bit awkward.  If your objective was to produce stratum-specific estimates, then allocating effort within the strata of interest would have been a safer route.  Note this discussion on our list back in 2014 about a design similar to yours:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/tiago%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/owhsicU2888/vspY9W6fJF8J

Also note that your data seem to tell you that birds hardly use 4 of your habitat types.  Your inference about burrow density in the strata with <50 detections produce CVs > 0.30, hence pretty wide confidence intervals.  Contribution of strata 1, 4, 6 and 7 to the overall abundance estimate is ~5%.
